newsitem.title: MOROCCO: U.S. envoy says talks with Arafat "very thorough".
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy says talks with Arafat "very thorough".

text.p: U.S. envoy Dennis Ross left Morocco on Thursday after holding what he called "very thorough" talks on the troubled Middle East peace process with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

Neither Ross nor Arafat made any comment to reporters after nearly two hours of talks, underlining the delicate task facing U.S. President Bill Clinton's special envoy in salvaging the peace process threatened by Jewish settlements in Jerusalem and violence.
But Ross, who met Moroccan King Hassan after arriving on Wednesday night, later termed his talks with Arafat as "a very thorough discussion".

In a statement issued by the U.S. embassy, he added: "The purpose of my mission is to make an assessment of the situation in the Middle East for the president and the secretary of state and to report back to them by this weekend."
Ross was to have talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on the threatened peace process in the Middle East.
Arafat and Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa made clear before Ross arrived at Arafat's villa that he would be left in no doubt over Arab anger with the policies of Netanyahu.

Moussa told reporters he had talked with the Saudi, Syrian, Gulf and North African foreign ministers -- in Rabat to attend a meeting of the Al-Qods (Jerusalem) committee -- and had briefed Arafat on their views.

"Everybody, all of us, are really disturbed over what is going on in Jerusalem. This is the issue. This is the reason why all the repercussions which took place in the occupied territories and in the Middle East have occurred," he said.
The minister was referring to West Bank clashes which entered an eighth day on Thursday, triggered by Israel starting building work on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
A suicide bomber blew himself up in Tel Aviv last Friday, killing three Israelis, and a Hamas spokesman in an interview published the next day said Israel must expect more bombings.
An Arab diplomat told Reuters that the Palestinians wanted Ross to put pressure on Israel to halt work on the settlement.
"If they can freeze this settlement it will be easier to return to negotiations," he said.
After leaving Morocco, Ross was due to hold talks in Israel with Netanyahu.
Moussa emphasised the Arab view that Israeli policies were to blame for the crisis.
"The problems lies, begins, stems from the policy of settlements in Jerusalem and in the occupied territories. We cannot accept a deviation from that point.

"If we deal with that point, and deal properly with it, I believe, and all of us believe, that this will lead to the resumption of a better and more conducive atmosphere for the negotiations and process of peace in general," Moussa said.

"The issue of Jerusalem is sensitive. We cannot accept this way of dealing with the issue of Jerusalem, dealing with us as Arabs, with the agreements, the conventions and the law that governs this situation," Moussa said.
Moussa and Arafat spent nearly 30 minutes in their talks, with the Egyptian minister leaving minutes before Ross arrived with U.S. ambassador to Morocco Marc Ginsberg.
Arafat, before going into his talks with Ross, emphasised past U.S. involvement in the peace process. He told reporters:

"We...feel the crime of the Israelis against Jerusalem, the judaisation of Jerusalem, building settlements...is a real crime against the peace process and the agreements signed in the White House under the supervision of President Clinton, against the letter of guarantees which we had received in Madrid from the American administration, signed by (former U.S. Secretary of State) Mr (James) Baker and completely against international legality."
